title: A little rule (ch. 73)
hook: Benedict calls it a little rule for beginners

segments.voice: Yesterday, good zeal: honor others first, and carry their weaknesses with patience. Your line was bear with each other. Did a habit pass without a word from you? Day one thousand two hundred four.

A man writes out a rule for a whole way of life. Prayer through the day and night, work, food, sleep, the sick, the guests, the tools, the vows, what to do when someone is late for dinner. Then he reaches the final page. A reader might expect a flourish here: this is the complete path, follow it and you'll arrive. Benedict writes something close to the opposite. He calls the whole thing a little rule, written for beginners. Today, the Rule's closing chapter, and the end of many days spent inside it.
screen: `A WHOLE WAY OF LIFE, WRITTEN DOWN.` → `THE FINAL PAGE.` → `A LITTLE RULE, FOR BEGINNERS.`

segments.voice: Chapter seventy-three opens with an admission. Benedict says he wrote this Rule so that, by keeping it, monks might show at least some measure of good living and a beginning of the monastic life. A beginning, not a finish line. For anyone hurrying on toward something more, he says, there are better teachers. And then he points away from himself. First, to Scripture: what page, what word of the Old and New Testaments, he asks, is not a true guide for human life? Then to the writers who came before him: the holy fathers, the Conferences and Institutes of John Cassian, the lives of the desert monks, the rule of Saint Basil. Next to those, he says, his own work is small. Then the last sentence, to whoever is reading: if you are hurrying toward your heavenly home, keep, with Christ's help, this little rule for beginners, and then, under God's protection, you will reach the greater heights he has just named. These past days brought hours set aside for reading, guests received as Christ, kitchen tools treated like vessels of the altar, the sick put first, a promise to stay, and the patience to bear each other. All of that, Benedict calls a start. The humility of the ladder chapter turns out to be the author's own. He never claims to have finished the climb. And the beginner is not someone who will soon stop being one. In the Prologue, Benedict called his monastery a school. Here at the end, he's still enrolling students. The Rule closes with a door left open: always beginning.
screen: `A BEGINNING, NOT A FINISH LINE.` · `HE POINTS TO SCRIPTURE AND THE FATHERS.` · `A WEEK OF THE RULE, CALLED A START.` · then, large: `THIS LITTLE RULE FOR BEGINNERS.` · then: `STILL ENROLLING STUDENTS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: begin again. Settle, and breathe. Think of one thing from these chapters you meant to try and didn't, or tried once and dropped. The hour of reading. The guest. The patience. Don't grade yourself. Just pick it up again, right now, the way a beginner picks up a pencil on the first day of school. Breathe in as if this is the first breath of the day. Breathe out and let the last attempt go. If you pray, you can borrow a psalm line from the Douay-Rheims: "Now have I begun." The bell holds the time.
A little rule. Benedict's own name for his Rule in its closing chapter: a small rule, written for beginners, pointing beyond itself to Scripture and the fathers. Today's word.
Your line: always beginning. Today, when something goes wrong, skip the verdict on yourself and just start the next try. Day one thousand two hundred four.

howItsDone: Benedictines speak of the monastic life as a lifelong beginning, and the Rule, ending with this chapter, is read through again from the Prologue in houses that read it in a cycle.

fork.setup: you've written a whole rule of life and reached the last page. how do you end it?
options: declare it the complete and perfect way.
call it a little rule for beginners, and point to greater teachers.
end with a list of punishments for those who ignore it.
fork.reveal: Benedict calls it a little rule for beginners, and names Scripture, Cassian, the desert fathers and Basil as guides to the heights.

original.note: Latin: rule, the word Benedict uses for his whole book, small as he calls it.

trapdoor: what you thought: a rule is a list of dos and don'ts.
what it means: Benedict's Rule calls itself a little rule for beginners, a start toward greater heights.
what a scholar hears: chapter seventy-three names Cassian's Conferences and Institutes and the rule of Basil as fuller guides.

notes: The Rule is paraphrased. Check the summary of ch. 73: the Rule written so that by observing it monks show some uprightness of life and a beginning of monastic life; for those hastening to perfection, the teachings of the holy fathers; 'what page or word of the Old and New Testament is not a most unerring rule for human life?'; the Conferences and Institutes, the Lives of the Fathers, the rule of our holy father Basil; 'this minimal rule for beginners'; with God's protection you will reach the loftier heights.

Week-end review covers days 1198–1203 (reading, guests, tools, the sick, stability, good zeal). 'The humility of the ladder chapter' refers to day 1194. 'In the Prologue, Benedict called his monastery a school' refers to day 1188 ('a school for the Lord's service').

Practice offers Psalm 76:11 (Douay) 'Now have I begun' as an optional prayer line; it is not quoted in the Rule. Confirm Douay wording ('And I said, Now have I begun: this is the change of the right hand of the most High').
howItsDone: the claim that the Rule is read through again from the Prologue after ch. 73 reflects the cycle of daily reading in many houses; confirm wording.
Editor pass: removed 'a week' (the Rule block ran longer than a week) and the stock line 'here's what's striking'; howItsDone no longer implies every house rereads the Rule.
